title: Soundcheck
subtitle: Stars Between the Strings · Chapter 22 of 40
content:
The microphone made Greg sound like an angry duck.

He leaned toward it, said, "Check, one, two," and the speaker answered with a noise that sent a pair of gulls flying from the roof. I nearly fell off the edge of the low stage laughing.

"Love that for us," he said, looking up at the sound technician. "A new genre."

The Beach City boardwalk was busy even before lunch. The fundraiser organizers had arranged folding chairs and a donation table. Someone was carrying a box of paper cups up the steps while another volunteer tried to stop the wind from taking the event schedule into the ocean.

The technician crouched to examine the cable. The plug was cracked.

"That needs replacing, not twisting until it works," she said.

Greg looked guilty. "I might have been planning to twist it."

"I could tell."

"I'm tagging this for the scrap box," the technician said. "If the damaged lead gets mixed with the spares, somebody will try it again."

Greg rubbed his thumb along the worn edge of his guitar case. "Well, at least the goose noises weren't all my fault. That's good news for my musical reputation."

She didn't laugh. She took the lead out of his hand.

"Seriously. You could short the channel into the stand. This isn't a funny sound effect."

The smile left his face. "Okay. Sorry. Didn't know it was that bad."

The organizer asked whether the delay would cost them a song. Greg started to promise that it wouldn't, then stopped and looked at the rating on the spare amp.

"I can play acoustic while she tests the gear," he offered. "But don't put a full electric set on the sign until we know we can do it."

The organizer looked disappointed.

"People came for the old hits."

"Some of them did." Greg shrugged. "They still get me. That's either a bargain or a warning."

I helped mark the cable route behind the platform. Greg wrote FAILED on the red tag in huge letters and added a tiny frowning guitar.

"You gave it a personality," I said.

"Yeah. Now nobody invites it back."

While the technician went for the replacement, he tapped a quiet rhythm with the heel of his shoe. The waiting made him restless in a way it never made Iroh restless. He was a musician looking for the moment he could turn anxiety into a sound rather than a maxim.

I helped move the spare chairs out of the walkway while she fetched a replacement. The event's organizer, a man in a pale shirt, came over to ask Greg whether he would stick to the old popular songs. They'd promised the donors familiar material.

Greg rubbed the back of his neck. "I was thinking of doing one new one."

"People are coming to hear Mr. Universe. You know, the fun stuff."

I saw the way his smile remained in place even after the rest of his face went quiet.

"Could we talk about the running order after the cable's fixed?" I asked.

The organizer checked his watch, sighed, and agreed.

Greg stayed behind on the stage, looking at the set list. He had written my name beside the last song because we'd practiced a little harmony together. I didn't know whether I was more frightened of singing in public or of disappointing him.

"You don't have to do it," he said, catching me looking.

"I want to. I just don't want to make a fool of us."

"We're gonna be on stage. Making a fool of ourselves is sort of the deal."

The replacement cable arrived. The technician taped down the cord where it crossed the rear stage, then asked everyone to test the sound with the actual number of instruments we'd use.

Greg played the first chord. This time it sounded like a guitar.

"Unbelievable," he said. "Technology."

I took my place beside him. The harmony was rough at first, because I came in a beat late. He stopped, but instead of apologizing for me, he asked where I wanted the cue.

"Look at me before the second line," I said.

He nodded, and we tried again. It worked. That tiny accommodation felt larger than the whole stage.

The organizer returned. He had heard the rehearsal. "That new song doesn't sound like your old work."

"No," Greg said.

"Wouldn't a crowd-pleaser be safer?"

Greg glanced at me, then back at the man. "I can play the songs people know. But I want one that means something to me now."

The organizer looked at the donation table and the sparse rows of chairs.

"One new song," he conceded. "Please don't turn the rest into an experiment."

Greg agreed. He wasn't happy about the compromise, but it gave the set somewhere to begin.

The organizer called just as we were throwing away the lemonade cups.

"One more thing," he said, looking anxious. "The donor wants a photograph of the two of you before the show. Something romantic. It might bring in more money."

Greg stared at him. I felt my shoulders rise.

"We can take a photograph of the event," I said. "Of people who agree to be in it."

The organizer glanced toward the stage. "They're giving us a lot."

"I know. But a donation doesn't buy our relationship."

Greg took a breath. "Look, I want the instruments repaired too. That's why I said yes to playing. I didn't say yes to putting Jasper on a poster."

The man looked embarrassed, not cruel. He scratched a line off the clipboard and asked if a picture of the newly repaired instruments would work instead. We suggested he ask the volunteers first.

After he left, Greg leaned against the railing.

"I almost said yes because I didn't want to sound ungrateful," he admitted.

"That wouldn't make you a bad person. I'm glad you stopped."

He rubbed his hand over his face. "You were clear about being ethically non-monogamous and preferring polyamory from the start. I don't want to turn our relationship into the kind of story where somebody wins you."

"Then don't."

He laughed softly. "Simple as that?"

"Not simple. Just the next thing to do."

We went back to the stage and helped the technician test the replacement cable. She had us stand at different positions while Greg spoke into the microphone, so everyone could hear whether the crackling had stopped. It had.

"Good," she said. "Now the duck can retire."

Greg looked offended. "That was my experimental sound."

I laughed, and when he reached for my hand I took it. The music night would still happen, and we could still be seen together without being offered as the prize for a successful fundraiser.

We had forty minutes before the doors opened. Greg asked me to walk along the boardwalk with him. We bought lemonade from a stall and sat where the sea breeze wasn't quite strong enough to steal the cups.

"That guy hit a nerve," I said.

He stared out at the water. "Sometimes I feel like everyone's still waiting for the kid who thought a stage would fix his life. And I don't want to disappoint them."

"Does that include me?"

He looked shocked. "No! I mean, I hope not."

"You can disappoint me. You just have to talk to me about it."

"That's a terrible marketing pitch."

"Very niche audience."

He laughed, then touched the back of my hand. "You really want to sing?"

"I do. Not because I'm trying to prove I'm your only person."

"I know."

We had talked about my ethical non-monogamy and preference for polyamory long before this day. I could love him and others without asking a crowd to vote on which relationship counted. But I also wanted to be here for his performance, and I wanted to make that choice without it turning into a grand declaration.

The fundraiser began. There were too few chairs at first and then somehow too many people. The technician kept the levels sensible, and the organizer stopped trying to change the set once the first song had started.

Greg was nervous for half a verse. Then he relaxed into the music. He made one joke about the terrible microphone, and the technician called back that she was charging him extra for emotional distress.

When the final song came, he looked at me before the second line.

I came in on time.

The applause wasn't enormous. A little kid near the front danced anyway, with the wholehearted confidence of someone who had never been told to be embarrassed. The donation table collected enough to repair the community instruments they'd brought out for the event.

Backstage, Greg hugged me and then stepped back.

"Can I kiss you?" he asked.

"Yes."

It was brief and a little clumsy because I was still holding the second guitar. He laughed into my hair, and I wanted to stay there for a whole minute longer.

Then the technician asked us to help coil the cables. We did. The organizer thanked the volunteers by name rather than calling them a single happy family. Greg copied the set list for his notebook and left my name where it was.

On the walk home, he took my hand.

"Same time next gig?"

"Ask me when you've got a date."

"Right. Consent and calendars. I'm learning."

"So am I."
